Speaker: Pelias
Notes: In his speech, however, Pelias pretends to feel pity for Phrixus and his fate.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: Before his speech, it is mentioned that Jason is happy because of the eagle augury (1.161). In his speech, however, his thirst for action seems to be the prevalent emotional state, but it is also important to note that Jason wants to persuade Acastus to join the expedition in order to seek revenge against Pelias (cf. 1.152-155).

Speaker: Aeson
Notes: In this instance, the tag “infatuation” is used for an emotional state that would rather be described as an expression of familial love (cf. 1.348-349).

Speaker: Fama
Notes: Fama’s joyful demeanor when she sets off to Lemnos to wreak havoc (2.135) can also be interpreted as malevolence.

Speaker: Venus-Dryope
Notes: In this case, the change from a sad to a furious state of mind already occurs during the speech itself (cf. 2.180-181).

Speaker: Venus
Notes: It is not clear if Venus is still disguised as the Lemnian woman Dryope at this point or not, for this discussion see Schirner 2023, 694 n. 804 with further references.

Speaker: Hypsipyle
Notes: Hypsipyle’s speech could also be interpreted as an expression of pity towards her father.

Speaker: Hypsipyle
Notes: In her short prayer to Bacchus, Hypsipyle’s sense of guilt is also recognizable.

Speaker: Hypsipyle
Notes: In her speech, Hypsipyle also shows feelings of guilt and worry about her father’s fate.

Speaker: Hesione
Notes: Before her speech, Hesione shows signs of fear and shame (cf. 2.470).

Speaker: Laomedon
Notes: In his speech, however, Laomedon hides his negative feelings and agenda and promises Hercules rewards for saving his daughter Hesione.

Speaker: Juno
Notes: In her speech, however, Juno pretends to be worried about the situation in Colchis.

Speaker: Juno
Notes: In her speech, however, Juno feigns concern for the nymph Dryope, pretending to have destined Hylas to be her husband.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: Jason is worried about Hercules’ fate and allows the group to decide whether they want to resume searching for their lost comrade or to set sail. Before Jason’s speech, however, it is mentioned that Tiphys’ request to leave has already changed Jason’s mind (3.615-616). For this problem and further references see Schirner 2023, 554.

Speaker: Telamon
Notes: Besides anger, astonishment, sadness, and grief are also important components of Telamon’s emotional state before his speech (cf. 3.692-695).

Speaker: Jupiter
Notes: Before his angry speech directed at Juno, pity towards Hercules is already an important element of Jupiter’s emotional state (cf. 4.2).

Speaker: Dymas
Notes: Before his speech, not only fear but also sadness and grief constitute important components of Dymas’ emotional state (cf. 4.135-136).

Speaker: Juno
Notes: Concerned about her marriage (4.354), Juno asks Jupiter for the cow into which he had transformed Io. Before her plea for the cow, however, Juno fakes a happy attitude (4.359).

Speaker: Zetes
Notes: In Zetes’ speech, pity for Phineus is also relevant (4.469-470).

Speaker: Phineus
Notes: Before his speech, Phineus’ calm and dignified demeanor is described (4.551-552). In his speech, however, he talks about future endeavors and the dangerous situations the Argonauts will have to face.

Speaker: Phineus
Notes: Phineus is thankful for his rescue, but he also harbors some doubt that the Harpies are really gone (cf. 4.633-634).

Speaker: Jason
Notes: Jason is included in the scared group before his speech (4.637-643); in his speech, however, he admonishes the men to be brave.

Speaker: Minerva
Notes: The narrator and Juno call Minerva worried (5.280-281, 286); in her speech, however, Minerva seems primarily eager to go to war.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: Jason is described as fearful and worried before his speech (5.302-311); in his address, however, he admonishes the men to be optimistic and brave.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: In his speech to Medea, however, Jason presents himself as someone who is worried and in need of help (cf. 5.389-390).

Speaker: Aeetes
Notes: Aeetes’ speech, however, is friendly (cf. also 5.533-534), as he offers Jason a deal of how to earn the golden fleece.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: In the beginning of his short speech, however, Jason laments the new challenge Aeetes confronted him with (5.542-545).

Speaker: Juno
Notes: In this passage, Juno appears as Medea’s sister Chalciope, but there is no significant discrepancy between her authentic feelings and her displayed emotions.

Speaker: Juno
Notes: In her speech, Juno, disguised as Chalciope, intends to draw Medea’s attention towards Jason.

Speaker: Medea
Notes: Before her speech, Medea’s growing infatuation for Jason and her worried state of mind are relevant (6.660-674). In her speech, her concern for Jason is the crucial factor.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: In his speech to Aeetes, Jason appears courageous and determined. Before his speech, however, he is shocked, sad, angry and stunned (7.81-86).

Speaker: Medea
Notes: Medea is joyful because of the arrival of her aunt Circe (who is, in fact, the disguised goddess Venus), but in her speech she also complains about the long absence of her aunt.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: The speaker is not the “real” Jason, but the fake one that is part of Venus-Circe’s deceitful speech.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: While the beginning of Jason’s speech could somehow be interpreted as an expression of helplessness on Jason’s part (7.413-414), his speech is primarily characterized by reproaches and a defiant attitude. After his speech, however, it is – probably from Medea’s point of view – stated that he is humbly asking for help (7.431). Before his speech, it is also mentioned that he comforts Medea by his words; this does, however, not match with the content of the speech itself. For this discussion and further references see Schirner 2023, 432-434.

Speaker: Medea
Notes: Before her speech, shame is also an important part of Medea’s emotional constitution (cf. 7.435). In her speech, she also reproaches Jason for being dependent on her help (7.437-439).

Speaker: Jason
Notes: In addition to infatuation, “sad shame” (7.514) is also an element of Jason’s emotional state after his speech.

Speaker: Medea
Notes: In addition to infatuation, “sad shame” (7.514) is also an element of Medea’s emotional state before her speech. In this speech, however, Medea announces dangerous challenges that Jason has to overcome.

Speaker: Medea
Notes: Before her speech, Medea seems amused by Jason’s fear of the dragon (under the assumption that the reading trahit ridens, V. Fl. 7.531, “she pulls him away, laughing”, is the correct one, cf. Schirner 2023, 229-230). In her speech, Medea seems again worried about Jason.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: Jason is worried about stealing the golden fleece from the dragon (8.24, 44). In his speech, he asks Medea for help, but he also emphasizes his feelings for her (which may or may not be sincere; for this discussion and further references see Schirner 2023, 758).

Speaker: Medea
Notes: Medea’s speech to Jason also includes threatening elements (cf. 8.48-50).

Speaker: Medea
Notes: Medea’s sense of guilt is evident in the speech she utters after she has put the dragon to sleep (8.95-108). In her short instruction towards Jason following this speech (8.110-111), this sentiment is not present anymore.

Speaker: Medea
Notes: After her speech, Medea is in some kind of fearful frenzy (cf. 8.445-450).

Speaker: Jason
Notes: Before his speech (of which only one verse has been transmitted), shame is also a part of Jason’s emotional state (8.464).
